fullPassage: When a country is in a recession, should its government spend more money or less? On a surface level, there are good arguments for each. The best argument for spending more money to get out of a bad economic situation was the 1930s Great Depression in the United States, where massively increased federal spending under President Franklin D. Roosevelt appeared to guide the economy back on track by loaning public-sector money into the private sector to create jobs and promote social welfare. This is traditionally the approach favored by the British economist John Maynard Keynes, whose overall system, referred to as Keynesian economics, is the most widely accepted economic philosophy in Western academic circles. Neoliberalism favors an alternate approach called austerity. Inspired by supply-side economics, austerity operates on the belief that if you cut taxes, especially for investors and corporations, it will increase private-sector spending and investment, precluding the need for dramatic government intervention. Of course, in order to cut taxes you need to decrease government spending. This creates an unpopular situation where a large number of people, already driven into poverty during a recession, find that their government support system is also getting smaller. Austerity hasn't produced a clear success story yet. History has shown so far that investors tend to hold on to their money during recessions, which are also not generally regarded as ideal times for private corporations to dramatically expand their workforce. But neoliberals continue to experiment with different austerity policies, looking for a private-sector, supply-side solution to recessions that can rescue an economy without increasing taxes or the size of the government.

When a country is in a recession, should its government spend more money or less?

(A) This creates an unpopular situation where a large number of people, already driven into poverty during a recession, find that their government support system is also getting smaller.

(B) The best argument for spending more money to get out of a bad economic situation was the 1930s Great Depression in the United States, where massively increased federal spending under President Franklin D. Roosevelt appeared to guide the economy back on track by loaning public-sector money into the private sector to create jobs and promote social welfare.

(C) Neoliberalism favors an alternate approach called austerity. Inspired by supply-side economics, austerity operates on the belief that if you cut taxes, especially for investors and corporations, it will increase private-sector spending and investment, precluding the need for dramatic government intervention.

det.korean: 올바른 순서: (B) 케인스식 지출 확대 논거 → (C) 대안인 긴축정책 소개 → (A) 긴축정책의 부작용
det.analysis:
① (A) - (B) - (C)
→ (A)는 '이것(This)이 불인기 상황을 만든다'로 시작하여, 바로 앞에 긴축정책이 세금과 지출을 줄인다는 설명이 먼저 나와야 함. 도입문 직후에 올 수 없음

② (B) - (C) - (A) ← 정답
→ 도입문: 정부가 돈을 더 쓸지 덜 쓸지의 문제 → (B): 더 쓰는 쪽(케인스식)의 대표 사례인 대공황 시기 루즈벨트의 재정 확대 → (C): Neoliberalism favors an alternate approach(대안인 긴축정책)로 전환, 세금 인하와 정부 개입 축소 설명 → (A): This creates an unpopular situation(이것)으로 (C)의 지출 축소를 이어받아 그 부작용(빈곤층 지원 축소) 설명

③ (C) - (B) - (A)
→ (C)가 먼저 오면 '대안(alternate approach)'이라는 표현이 아직 제시되지 않은 첫 번째 주장(B)을 가리킬 수 없어 논리 붕괴

④ (C) - (A) - (B)
→ (A)의 'This'가 (C)의 지출 축소를 받아야 하는데 (B)가 뒤로 밀려 전체 대조 구조가 무너짐
det.tip: This creates an unpopular situation의 This는 바로 앞 문장의 '정부 지출 축소' 내용을 가리키는 지시사다.

questions.passage: When a country is in a recession, should its government spend more money or less? On a surface level, there are good arguments for each. The best argument for spending more money to get out of a bad economic situation was the 1930s Great Depression in the United States, where massively increased federal spending under President Franklin D. Roosevelt appeared to guide the economy back on track by loaning public-sector money into the private sector to create jobs and promote social welfare. This is traditionally the approach favored by the British economist John Maynard Keynes, whose overall system, referred to as Keynesian economics, is the most widely accepted economic philosophy in Western academic circles. Neoliberalism favors an alternate approach called austerity. Inspired by supply-side economics, austerity operates on the belief that if you cut taxes, especially for investors and corporations, it will increase private-sector spending and investment, precluding the need for dramatic government intervention. Of course, in order to cut taxes you need to decrease government spending. This creates an unpopular situation where a large number of people, already driven into poverty during a recession, find that their government support system is also getting smaller. Austerity hasn't produced a clear success story yet. History has shown so far that investors tend to hold on to their money during recessions, which are also not generally regarded as ideal times for private corporations to dramatically expand their workforce. But neoliberals continue to experiment with different austerity policies, looking for a private-sector, __________ without increasing taxes or the size of the government.
